archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose point differential, efficiency and top-10 passing offense describe a winning club, while a 3-5 record carries the cost of close losses and leaky big-play defense.

report.headline: A winning team's profile trapped in a 3-5 record by close-game misses
report.take:
Houston is not a 3-5 team in the way its record suggests. It has outscored opponents by 17 points, and its differential implies 4.8 wins rather than three. Its -1.82 wins over expected ranks 30th, meaning only two teams have been unluckier relative to their scoring margin. Net EPA sits 13th. All but one of the losses came by a single score, and the 0.2 one-score win rate ranks 26th. That is mostly a coin-flip problem, not a talent problem.

The identity has flipped from a year ago. The 2025 team won 12 games on a defense that ranked 2nd in EPA allowed and 2nd in points allowed, with an offense that ranked 22nd. This year the offense carries the team. It ranks 8th in EPA, 7th in passing EPA and 9th in scoring at 26.1 a game. C.J. Stroud has started every week behind a line that allows the 4th-lowest pressure rate. He has thrown for 2,251 yards, and the offense has committed only four turnovers. The defense has slipped to 17th, though the cause is narrow: it rarely breaks, but when it does, it breaks badly.

The numbers hide that split inside the defense. Houston leads the league with 29 sacks, ranks 2nd in sack rate and 7th in success rate allowed. It also allows the highest explosive-pass rate in football, ranks 24th on deep-pass EPA and gives up touchdowns on two-thirds of red-zone trips. That is a unit that wins most downs and then hands back a chunk play. The run game is the other drag: 3.32 yards a carry and a 29th-ranked rush success rate. Special teams that bleed EPA, a conservative 4th-down habit and 8 penalties a game add small taxes that decide one-score games.

The direction is encouraging. After a winless September, the passing game has posted big positive EPA in most games since. The 44-22 win in Los Angeles, with 391 passing yards and 8 sacks, was the most complete performance of the year. The schedule ahead includes Indianapolis, Washington, Philadelphia and Tennessee, all with losing records, plus a Jacksonville team Houston has already beaten on the road. A team this efficient should win more of its close games going forward. Even so, a 3-5 hole and a 6-2 division leader leave little slack.

strengths.title: A passing game built to last
strengths.body: Houston's offense ranks 7th in passing EPA, and it rests on a sturdy foundation. The line allows the 4th-lowest pressure rate and 5th-lowest QB hit rate, so Stroud gets clean pockets on a normal 2.865-second clock. This is a sharp jump from a 22nd-ranked offense in 2025, and the protection is the kind of trait that holds up. The one thing to monitor is depth at receiver, with Jaylin Noel lost for the season.

strengths.title: League-best pass rush
strengths.body: Houston leads the league in sacks and ranks 2nd in sack rate, despite only a middling 16th in pressure rate. That means the defense converts its pressure into sacks at a very high clip. Some of that efficiency will cool. Still, a 7th-ranked QB hit rate says the rush itself is real, and it keeps offenses behind the chains, which shows up in a 7th-ranked success rate allowed.

strengths.title: Ball security drives turnover edge
strengths.body: Houston's turnover differential ranks 8th even though the defense has forced just 8 takeaways. The edge comes almost entirely from an offense that has given the ball away only four times. Low-turnover passing tends to persist more than takeaway luck does. That makes this a healthier version of the turnover edge than the 2025 team's.

concerns.title: Defense gives up the big one
concerns.body: Houston allows the league's highest explosive-pass rate and ranks 24th on deep throws. That undercuts how often it wins on early downs. It also gives up touchdowns on 66.7% of red-zone trips, which turns modest drives into seven points. Losing starting safety Reed Blankenship to a concussion only thins the back end. This is a real flaw rather than noise, and it explains why a top sack defense still allows 24 points a game.

concerns.title: Run game stuck in the mud
concerns.body: The ground game averages 3.32 yards a carry and ranks 29th in success rate and 27th in yards before contact. That is a run-blocking problem, not game script, because the same line protects the passer superbly. It makes Houston one-dimensional late in games, when it needs to burn clock. That likely plays a part in the 23rd-ranked time of possession and the close-loss pattern. With David Montgomery out, Woody Marks carries more of it.

concerns.title: Small taxes losing close games
concerns.body: Several self-inflicted costs compound in one-score games. Special teams are negative, the team averages 8 penalties a game, and it ranks 29th in going for it on 4th down despite a top-10 offense. None of these is large alone. Together they help explain a 20% one-score win rate that efficiency says should be closer to even. Expect the win rate to drift up, but the habits will need to improve too.

trend.note: After a winless September with negative passing EPA in two of the first three games, the offense has posted big positive passing EPA in most games since. The 44-22 win at the Chargers was the high point. The home loss to the Giants as a 10-point favorite is the warning that the floor is still low.

nextGame.headline: Houston's league-best pass rush meets the league's worst pass protection
nextGame.body:
This matchup sets Houston's two best traits against Cleveland's two worst weaknesses. The Browns allow the highest sack rate and QB hit rate in the league, with 38 sacks taken. Houston leads the league in sacks. Cleveland's offense ranks 25th in EPA and 29th rushing it, so it struggles to stay ahead of the chains. On the other side, the Browns' defense is stout against the pass (9th in EPA) and gets home itself (26 sacks, 3rd). However, it ranks 29th against the run, allows the most explosive runs in the league and misses tackles more than anyone. A 5-4 record built on +1.62 wins over expected and a 0.714 one-score win rate flatters a team with a -3.9 point differential. The Book has Houston -4.5 with a 39.5 total, which projects a lower-scoring game than Houston usually plays.

Availability tilts toward Houston. Deshaun Watson is out with a concussion, so Shedeur Sanders makes his second straight start behind that leaky line. Starting DT Maliek Collins is also out, further weakening an already soft run defense. For Houston, David Montgomery's groin injury leaves Woody Marks as the lead back. Jaylin Noel is gone for the year, so the targets run through Dalton Schultz, Xavier Hutchinson and Nico Collins. The missing piece that matters most is safety Reed Blankenship, an 86%-snap starter, on a defense that already gives up too many deep balls.

waysToWin.title: Pass rush overwhelms Sanders
waysToWin.body: Cleveland gives up sacks at the league's worst rate, and Houston generates them at the 2nd-best rate. With a backup-level start at quarterback, drive-killing sacks should come often. That is what happened in the 8-sack game against the Chargers. If Houston turns pressure into long-yardage downs, a weak Browns offense rarely recovers.

waysToWin.title: Finally find a run game
waysToWin.body: Houston's ground game has been poor, but this is the matchup to fix it. Cleveland ranks 29th in rush EPA allowed, allows the most explosive runs and misses the most tackles, and it is without DT Maliek Collins. A few chunk runs from Marks would let Houston control the clock with a lead rather than leaning on Stroud against a good pass defense.

waysToWin.title: Clean protection keeps Stroud upright
waysToWin.body: The Browns' sack total is a real threat, but Houston's line allows the 4th-lowest pressure rate. If it holds up, Stroud can work the intermediate game and lean on Schultz. Cleveland has been stingy on WR1 targets but less so on tight ends and the third receiver.

waysToLose.title: Another one-score coin flip
waysToLose.body: A 39.5 total points to a tight, grinding game, which is exactly where Houston has failed this year and Cleveland has thrived. Cleveland's positive special-teams EPA against Houston's negative number is the kind of hidden edge that swings a close game. The same goes for a missed 4th-down chance.

waysToLose.title: Big plays over a thin secondary
waysToLose.body: Houston allows the league's highest explosive-pass rate, and its starting safety is out. A weak passing offense can still steal a game with two or three deep shots that beat the rush. Houston's red-zone defense would then need to hold, and it has rarely done that.

waysToLose.title: Getting out-physicaled on the ground
waysToLose.body: The Giants ran for 188 yards in Houston's worst loss, and the run defense ranks only 18th in EPA. If Cleveland hides Sanders behind a ground game and wins the possession battle, Houston's offense gets fewer chances against a top-10 pass defense.

nextGame.watch: Houston's pass rush against Cleveland's league-worst protection: if Sanders is under siege early, this one tilts quickly.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency is real enough to expect a better second half. A top-10 passing offense with elite protection and low turnovers tends to hold up. A pass rush this productive should keep the defense around league average even with the big-play leaks. The close-game record is the part most likely to regress in Houston's favor. The schedule helps: half of the remaining games come against teams with losing records, and the defense will face several of the weaker offenses in the league. Pittsburgh, Green Bay and the Jacksonville rematch are the hard ones.

What will not fix itself is the run game and the explosive-play defense. The sack rate will likely cool somewhat from its league-best pace. Houston needs to win most of the soft games to climb back toward a winning record, and catching Jacksonville for the division would require near-perfection. A wild-card push is realistic if the offense keeps its form.
swingFactors: Stroud's passing efficiency holding up as Noel's absence thins the receivers
Whether the defense cuts down explosive passes without Blankenship
Closing out one-score games, including the Jacksonville rematch

confidence.note: Only eight games, and the record is driven by close-game noise, but efficiency, differential and protection all point the same way.
